How do computers "see" the world? The mathematical foundation of computer vision lies in
 understanding how shapes and images transform—and this course will teach you that
 language from the ground up.
 Starting with the familiar geometry of high school (Euclidean), we'll discover how different
 types of transformations create entirely new geometries. You'll learn how allowing shapes to
 be scaled gives us Similarity Geometry, how parallel lines behave in Affine Geometry, and
 ultimately how Projective Geometry explains why railroad tracks appear to meet at the
 horizon—the same mathematics that lets computers reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D
 photographs.
 This isn't your typical geometry course. Following Felix Klein's revolutionary approach, we'll
 see geometry not as a collection of theorems about triangles and circles, but as the study of
 what stays the same when shapes transform. This unified view connects ancient Greek
 mathematics to cutting-edge computer vision applications like facial recognition, autonomous
 vehicles, and augmented reality.
 No advanced mathematics required—just high school algebra, basic calculus, and curiosity
 about how mathematical ideas connect. Through concrete examples and visual reasoning,
 you'll build intuition for concepts that usually appear only in graduate courses.
 
 This course sets the foundation for Computer Vision II, where you'll apply these geometric
